concerns.text: Eight months of gradually blurry near print in the right eye of a 71-year-old woman is clearly non-emergent, though clinicians may route initial assessment either to a primary-care physician visit (level 2) or directly to an outpatient optometrist or ophthalmologist (level 3).

A 3-week 1 cm soft rubbery thigh lump at a daily insulin injection site fits non-emergent insulin lipohypertrophy evaluation at a primary-care physician visit (level 2), though patients managed in a diabetes or endocrinology clinic may have injection sites and insulin dosing reviewed directly by their specialist (level 3).

Two years of floor clutter blocking the hallway and kitchen in a 67-year-old woman warrants structured cognitive behavioral therapy with an outpatient therapist (level 3), though clinicians also commonly begin with a primary-care physician visit to screen for late-life cognitive or medical contributors and coordinate home safety (level 2).

Six months of nightly loud snoring with witnessed 15-second breathing pauses in a 51-year-old man warrants diagnostic sleep testing via an outpatient sleep specialist (level 3), though without prior workup a primary-care physician visit to assess cardiovascular risk and order home sleep apnea testing first is equally standard (level 2).

Uncomplicated febrile pharyngitis (102 F for 2 days) developing a rough red chest rash and strawberry tongue in a 7-year-old boy is appropriately managed at a same-day outpatient clinic with rapid streptococcal testing and oral antibiotics (level 2), though some clinicians triage acute febrile pediatric rash with mucosal tongue changes to urgent emergency evaluation if same-day clinic testing is unavailable (level 4).

A 10-day soft 4 cm posterior elbow fluid pouch in a plumber who leans on his elbows warrants an outpatient clinic examination to confirm aseptic olecranon bursitis and exclude low-grade infection (level 2), though when non-tender and afebrile some clinicians advise trialing elbow padding and pressure offloading at home first (level 1).

An acute warm tender wedge-shaped erythematous breast patch with a 101 F fever at 3 weeks postpartum is managed as uncomplicated lactational mastitis at a same-day outpatient physician visit (level 2), though febrile postpartum breast infection sits near the urgent triage boundary where clinicians evaluate in the emergency department if same-day assessment is unavailable or systemic sepsis must be excluded (level 4).
